chunks: Types of rework on a PCB. The question: What sort of rework can be done on a PCB?
Rework comes in a few kinds, and each kind fits a different fault.
You can replace a part, add a wire to change a connection, change which parts are fitted, repair damaged copper, or clean up solder mess.
Think of fixing a road. Replacing a broken sign is swapping a part. Building a detour is adding a wire. Filling a pothole is repairing a lifted pad.
Sweeping up debris is cleaning off a solder bridge. A detour is fine for a slow footpath, but it adds extra distance, and on a fast highway that extra distance causes trouble.
A wire on a circuit is the same: harmless for slow signals, a problem for very fast ones.
Most bring-up fixes fall into one of five branches. The cheapest and safest branches (population changes) are the ones you can design in; the others need heat and skill.
Bodge wire (jumper): a thin wire added by hand to make a connection the board does not have.
Cut-and-jump: cutting a copper trace so a connection is removed, then adding a wire to connect somewhere else.
DNP (do not populate): a spot on the board left empty on purpose, so a part can be fitted later if needed. Inductance: how strongly a wire resists changes in current.
It only matters when the signal changes very fast. Lifted pad: a copper pad that has peeled off the board.
Suppose a reset signal was never connected to the chip that needs it. You solder a thin wire from the reset pad to the chip pin, and glue the wire down.
A 30 mm wire has about 30 nanohenries of inductance (a rough rule is 1 nanohenries per millimeter). At 1 megahertz that is only about 0.
19 ohms, and at 100 megahertz about 19 ohms. A reset line barely changes, so the wire is harmless. A 100 megahertz clock would be badly disturbed. That is the whole idea.

"I split rework into component replacement (through-hole, SMD, or BGA/QFN with a rework station), connection changes like cut-and-jump bodge wires, population changes like swapping values or fitting DNP parts, repairs of lifted pads or traces, and cleanup of bridges or coating.
Each has risks: wires add about a nanohenry per millimetre, so fine for slow signals and bad for fast ones, and every thermal cycle stresses the board."
